summary: Specifies the CLUE protocol, an application protocol that lets telepresence endpoints describe and negotiate a session. It builds on the requirements and framework produced by the IETF CLUE working group. It is an experimental specification and has a companion signaling document, RFC 8848.

plainLanguage.summary:
CLUE is the language two telepresence endpoints use to agree on what to send each other. One side says what cameras and encodings it has; the other side says which ones it wants to receive.

The messages are XML documents carried over an encrypted data channel, so the two sides can keep talking about the call while it is running.

subtitle: Telepresence endpoints describe and negotiate media streams over SCTP-over-DTLS.

tldr.problem: A telepresence session involves many choices about which cameras and encodings to send, and plain SDP cannot describe all of them, so the participants need another way to agree.
tldr.mechanism: CLUE is an XML-based application protocol. One side advertises the media captures it can offer, the other picks the ones it wants, and both sides exchange the messages over an encrypted data channel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines six messages, two state machines, a version and extension negotiation, and a set of response codes. It is an Experimental document, and RFC 8848 covers the signaling that sets the session up.

today: RFC 8847 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted. It is the protocol half of the CLUE set: RFC 8845 holds the framework, RFC 8846 the data model, RFC 8848 the signaling and SDP session establishment, and RFC 8850 the data channel.

sections.title: What CLUE Is For
sections.content:
The Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence protocol is an application protocol used by two CLUE Participants to enhance the experience of a multimedia telepresence session. It has two main goals. The first is to let a Media Provider announce its current telepresence capabilities to a Media Consumer in terms of available media captures, groups of encodings, simultaneity constraints and other information defined in RFC 8845. The second is to let the Media Consumer request the multimedia streams it wants from the offering Media Provider.

CLUE-capable endpoints are connected by a CLUE data channel, an SCTP-over-DTLS channel that is opened and established as described in RFC 8848 and RFC 8850. SCTP stands for Stream Control Transmission Protocol. The CLUE messages that flow over such a channel are described in this document, both syntactically and semantically. The companion document RFC 8848 deals with CLUE signaling details and with the SIP and Session Description Protocol session establishment phase.

The design of CLUE takes into account the requirements and the framework defined by the IETF CLUE Working Group. It exists because SDP alone cannot convey the information about the features of the flowing multimedia streams that are needed for a rendering experience that feels like being there.
sections.plainLanguage: CLUE answers a question SDP cannot: not just how to set up a call, but which of the many pictures and sounds the room can produce should actually be sent.

sections.title: The Roles and the Terms
sections.content:
A CLUE Participant is an entity able to use the CLUE protocol within a telepresence session. It can be an endpoint or an MCU, a Multipoint Control Unit, able to use the protocol. An Endpoint is a CLUE-capable device that is the logical point of final termination through receiving, decoding and rendering, and of initiation through capturing, encoding and sending of media streams. An endpoint consists of one or more physical devices that source and sink media streams, and it can be anything from a multiscreen and multicamera room to a handheld device.

A Media Capture is a source of media, for example from one or more capture devices or constructed from other media streams. A Capture Encoding is a specific encoding of a media capture, to be sent with RTP. A Stream is a capture encoding sent from a Media Provider to a Media Consumer with RTP.

Two roles are built on the CLUE Participant. A Media Provider is a participant able to send capture encodings. A Media Consumer is a participant able to receive capture encodings. In many cases a participant acts in both roles at once, and in a call between two participants there are then two separate exchanges: one to set up the media going from A to B, and one for the media going from B to A.
sections.plainLanguage: One side offers pictures and sounds, the other side asks for them, and usually each side does both at the same time.

sections.title: Three Phases of a Session
sections.content:
CLUE is a stateful client-server XML-based application protocol whose messages flow on a reliable and ordered SCTP-over-DTLS transport channel connecting two participants. Three main phases can be identified.

First comes establishment of the CLUE data channel. If that completes successfully, the participants are able to communicate and start the initiation phase.

Second comes the initiation phase, in which the participants agree on the protocol version and the extensions to be used during the session. The 'options' and 'optionsResponse' messages do that job, and the negotiation is done once per session and only at this stage. At the end of it, each participant starts its activity as a Media Provider and/or Media Consumer. The version is written as a major number and a minor number separated by a dot. Minor numbers denote backward-compatible changes within a major version, while different major numbers generally mean the implementations cannot talk to each other, so both sides must have a major version in common. Only the extensions that both sides support are allowed in the session.

Third comes the description and negotiation of the telepresence capabilities. The Media Provider first advertises its available media captures, encoding capabilities and simultaneity constraints in an 'advertisement' message. The Media Consumer then selects the streams it wants with a 'configure' message, which refers back to the information in the advertisement. The messages are designed with the Media Provider as the server side, because it produces the streams, and the Media Consumer as the client side, because it requests them.
sections.plainLanguage: The session runs in three steps: open the channel, agree on what you both understand, then agree on what to send. Only the third step happens over and over during the call.

sections.title: The Six CLUE Messages
sections.content:
Every CLUE message carries an optional clueId, which identifies the participant within the telepresence system, and a sequenceNr. The sender must increment the sequence number by one for each new message, and the receiver must remember the most recent number and answer with a 402 error if it receives an unexpected one, such as a gap or a repeat. Each participant keeps up to three independent streams of sequence numbers: one for the initiation phase, one for messages sent as a Media Provider, and one for messages sent as a Media Consumer. Every message also carries a mandatory protocol attribute fixed to the value CLUE and a mandatory v attribute carrying the protocol version, for example 1.3 or 2.0.

There are six messages. The 'options' message is sent by the Channel Initiator as soon as the data channel is ready and states whether the sender can act as a Media Provider or a Media Consumer, together with the list of supported versions and the list of supported extensions. The 'optionsResponse' message is the reply from the Channel Receiver, which selects the extensions it can support and determines the version to be used. An extension is described by a name, the XML schema where it is defined, and the protocol version it refers to.

The 'advertisement' message carries the media captures, encoding groups, capture scenes, simultaneous sets, global views and represented participants. A new advertisement completely replaces the previous one, so a provider can send a new one when its capabilities change mid-call. The 'ack' message is the consumer's acknowledgement of an advertisement and carries the sequence number of the advertisement it refers to. The 'configure' message lists the advertised captures the consumer wants to receive, with the list of capture encodings that represent the streams to be instantiated; it may also carry an 'ack' element that acknowledges the advertisement in the same message, and that element must not be present if a separate acknowledgement has already been sent. The 'configureResponse' message reports whether the request succeeded or failed, and there is no partial execution: if the provider understands every requested capture encoding except one, the whole command fails and nothing is instantiated.

Response codes are three digits whose first digit carries the meaning. Codes starting with 2 are successful, 3 report a problem with the XML content of the message and 4 a problem with the protocol semantics. Version 1 defines 200 for success, 300 for a generic low-level request error, 301 for bad syntax, 302 for an invalid value, 303 for conflicting values, 400 for semantic errors, 401 for an unsupported version, 402 for an unexpected sequence number, 403 for an invalid identifier, 404 for an expired advertisement and 405 for a subset choice that is not allowed. Codes starting with 1 are reserved for future major versions, and codes starting with 0 are not allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Six kinds of message do all the work: offer, answer, advertise, acknowledge, request and confirm. Each one carries a running number so that both sides can tell whether a message arrived in the right order.

sections.title: How the Participants Behave
sections.content:
The participant state machine starts in IDLE, where the data channel does not exist. When the channel is started it moves to CHANNEL SETUP, and on success to OPTIONS. A channel error or the end of the session sends it back to IDLE. In OPTIONS the participant agrees on the version and extensions. If it is the Channel Initiator it sends 'options' and waits for the answer; if it is the Channel Receiver it waits for 'options' and replies. Success moves it to ACTIVE, and a failure, which can be an error response, a timeout on either side, sends it back to IDLE. Once ACTIVE, the participant hands the sending and processing of messages to the two role state machines, and it must ignore any further 'options' or 'optionsResponse' that arrives.

The Media Provider state machine starts in ADV, where it prepares its advertisement. Sending the advertisement moves it to WAIT FOR ACK. A successful acknowledgement moves it to WAIT FOR CONF, while an error acknowledgement sends it back to ADV to prepare a new advertisement. A 'configure' that carries a successful acknowledgement moves it straight to CONF RESPONSE. If its telepresence settings change while it waits, it goes back to ADV. In CONF RESPONSE the provider processes the request: on success it sends a 200 response and moves to ESTABLISHED, and on error it sends an error response and goes back to WAIT FOR CONF.

The Media Consumer state machine starts in WAIT FOR ADV. When the advertisement arrives it moves to ADV PROCESSING, where the advertisement is parsed. On success it either sends an acknowledgement and moves to CONF, where it prepares the request, or it sends the request straight away with the acknowledgement included and moves to WAIT FOR CONF RESPONSE. On failure it sends an error acknowledgement and waits for a new advertisement. A successful 'configureResponse' moves the consumer to ESTABLISHED, while an error response sends it back to CONF to try again. While ESTABLISHED, the consumer can send a new 'configure' to change the call settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side follows a fixed script. The provider advertises, waits, answers, and settles; the consumer waits, chooses, asks, and checks. Any change to the room sends the provider back to the start of the script.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The CLUE framework and protocol were conceived from the outset around the security-by-design idea, and a number of requirements were standardized as mandatory across the whole set of CLUE documents: the use of cryptography and authentication, protection of all sensitive fields, mutual authentication between CLUE endpoints, the presence of authorization mechanisms, and native defenses against eavesdropping, selective modification, deletion and replay. The security of the individual components cannot be judged apart from the whole architecture.

Because the protocol lets a producer and a consumer negotiate a varied set of parameters for a session, it exposes a telepresence system to a range of threats, most of which the framework document discusses, both for two endpoints and for the case where an MCU is present. The framework also notes that the information carried in CLUE messages may be sensitive and should be accessed only by authenticated endpoints.

The RFC points out one extra exposure. Some information exchanged during the negotiation phase is not part of the data model, in particular the list of supported versions and extensions sent in the 'options' and 'optionsResponse' messages. A malicious participant might try to use it to build a detailed picture of a particular implementation, or to force the other party onto an outdated version that the attacker knows how to break. An implementation can choose not to announce everything it supports to avoid the leak, at the cost of interoperability. The OPTIONS state is only reached after the data channel has been set up successfully, so only authenticated parties can exchange those messages, which greatly reduces the exposed surface.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is built to run inside an encrypted channel between authenticated endpoints. The one extra risk the RFC points at is that the list of supported versions gives away clues about the software on the other end.
